board_events.text: Same average, opposite reliability
Identical mean, yet one vendor is reliable and one is a gamble.
Central tendency = WHERE the data sits. Dispersion = HOW SPREAD OUT it is.

board_events.text: Dispersion asks: how far, on average, do the observations live from the centre?
The crudest measure of spread: the range
Grouped data: (upper boundary of highest class) − (lower boundary of lowest class).
Useful first glance: “today's temperature ranged from 22°C to 41°C.”
Weakness: the range listens ONLY to the two extremes and ignores everything between.
The coefficient of range is unit-free, so it compares spread across different scales.
A smarter idea than the range
For every observation, measure how far it sits from a central value, then average those distances.
Key move: use DISTANCE. A value 5 below the centre is as “spread out” as one 5 above.
Drop the signs → take ABSOLUTE values, or the deviations cancel to exactly 0.

board_events.text: Mean deviation = the average of these absolute distances.
Where mean deviation falls short
Weakness 1: the modulus |x| has a sharp corner at 0 — it won't differentiate cleanly.
So mean deviation refuses to slot into further algebra and calculus.
This is exactly why the next subtopic switches to variance, which SQUARES deviations instead.
Weakness 2: M.D. depends on the anchor — about the mean vs about the median gives different values.
Deviation is smallest about the MEDIAN — a fact that powers many exam shortcuts.
M.D. of ungrouped data, step by step
About the MEAN — Step 1: find the mean, the anchor all distances are measured from.
Step 2: form each |x_i − x̄|.  Step 3: add them.  Step 4: divide by n.
About the MEDIAN: same steps, but Step 1 finds the median (sort, take middle value).
Why bother with the median? It gives the smallest, most honest mean deviation the data can offer.

segments.text: <curious>Let's open the chapter with a small puzzle from your local vegetable market. Two vendors, Ramesh and Suresh, quote tomato prices over a week.
Ramesh quotes twenty eight, thirty, twenty nine, thirty one, and thirty rupees. Punch these into a calculator and the average comes out to twenty nine point six rupees per kilo.
Now Suresh: fourteen, forty six, twelve, forty eight, and thirty. Add them up, divide, and you get the exact same average, twenty nine point six rupees. Identical on paper.

But nobody would call these two vendors the same. Ramesh is boringly reliable, Suresh is a total gamble. The average has completely hidden the one thing that separates them, how scattered the prices are.
This is the key split. Central tendency, that's your mean, median and mode, tells you where the data sits. Dispersion tells you how tightly or loosely the observations huddle around that centre.

Look at the picture. Both number lines share the same mean, marked by the red dashed line. On top, Ramesh's prices cluster into a tight little knot. Below, Suresh's dots fling themselves to the far corners.
So dispersion is just a fair way of answering one question: how far, on average, do the dots live from home? That single question drives this entire chapter.
There's a whole hierarchy of ways to measure spread, and the crudest one is the range. It is simply the gap between the largest and the smallest observation.
In symbols, range equals x maximum minus x minimum. That's it, subtract the smallest value from the largest, and you have an instant sense of the total width of your data.
For grouped or continuous data there's a small tweak. You take the upper boundary of the highest class and subtract the lower boundary of the lowest class.
The range is genuinely useful as a first glance. When a weather report says today's temperature ranged from twenty two to forty one degrees, that number tells you something real about the day.

<chuckle>But the range is a bit of a drama queen. It listens only to the two most extreme values and completely ignores everything in between. One freak observation, and the range lies about the whole set.
To compare spread fairly across data sets of different scales, we use the coefficient of range: x max minus x min, divided by x max plus x min. Same-unit quantities on top and bottom.

Because it divides one same-unit quantity by another, the coefficient of range is a pure number with no units. That lets you compare, say, the spread of rupees against the spread of marks on a level field.
The range wastes almost all your data. A smarter idea is this: for every single observation, measure how far it sits from a central value, and then average all those distances.

Now here's the subtle move, and it hinges on one word, distance. A value sitting five units below the mean is just as spread out as one sitting five units above it. Direction shouldn't matter, only how far.
So we deliberately throw away the plus and minus signs. We take the absolute value of each deviation. A gap of minus five and a gap of plus five both count as a distance of five.
<whisper>Here's why this is not optional. The deviations from the mean always, always add up to exactly zero, that's a defining property of the mean itself.

You can see it written on the board: the sum of x i minus x bar is always zero. If we didn't take absolute values, our spread measure would report zero for every data set on earth, completely useless.
Look at the picture. From a chosen central point a, each observation sends out a little arrow whose length is the distance, x i minus a in absolute value.
The mean deviation is nothing more than the average length of all these distance arrows. That's the whole concept in one sentence.
Mean deviation is a real improvement on the range, but it carries two honest weaknesses you should keep in your head.
The first is mathematical. The absolute-value sign is clumsy. The function mod x has a sharp corner at zero, and you cannot differentiate it cleanly at that point.
Because of that corner, mean deviation simply refuses to slot into further algebra and calculus. It's a dead end if you want to build more theory on top of it.

And that is precisely why the very next subtopic abandons mean deviation in favour of variance and standard deviation, which square the deviations instead of taking absolute values, squaring is smooth everywhere.
The second weakness: mean deviation is only as meaningful as the central value you anchor it to. The same data set has a different mean deviation about its mean than about its median.
And here is the beautiful fact we'll prove later, written on the board: the sum of absolute deviations is smallest when you measure about the median.
<whisper>So the deviation is genuinely least about the median, not the mean. That quiet fact powers a lot of clever exam shortcuts, so lock it away now.
Mean deviation is computed, not derived, so let's nail the exact step-by-step procedure for ungrouped data, first about the mean.
Step one, find the mean. This is your anchor, the central value that every distance is going to be measured from. No anchor, no deviation.
The mean is x bar equals one over n times the sum of all the x i. Just add every observation and divide by how many there are.

Step two, form each absolute deviation, mod of x i minus x bar. Step three, add all those absolute deviations together to get the total scatter. Step four, divide by n to turn total scatter into an average.
Putting it together: mean deviation about the mean equals one over n, times the sum of the absolute deviations. Dividing by n is what makes the measure comparable across data sets of different sizes.

Now, about the median, the procedure is identical with one change. In step one, instead of the mean, you find the median: sort the data, take the middle value for odd n, or the average of the two middle values for even n.
Why go to that trouble? Because the median minimises the total absolute deviation. Measuring about it gives you the smallest, most honest mean deviation the data can possibly offer.

segments.text: <curious>Chalo chapter ki shuruaat ek chhote se puzzle se karte hain, aapke local sabzi mandi se. Do vendors hain, Ramesh aur Suresh, jo hafte bhar tomato ke daam batate hain.
Ramesh bolta hai twenty eight, thirty, twenty nine, thirty one, aur thirty rupees. Calculator mein daalo toh average nikalta hai twenty nine point six rupees per kilo.
Ab Suresh: fourteen, forty six, twelve, forty eight, aur thirty. Jod ke divide karo toh bilkul wahi average aata hai, twenty nine point six rupees. Paper pe dono same.
Lekin koi bhi in dono vendors ko ek jaisa nahi kahega. Ramesh reliable hai, Suresh ek gamble hai. Average ne wo cheez chhupa di jo inhe alag karti hai, yaani prices kitni bikhri hui hain.

Yahi main baat hai. Central tendency, matlab mean, median aur mode, batata hai ki data kahaan baitha hai. Dispersion batata hai ki observations us centre ke aas-paas kitni tightly ya loosely jama hain.
Picture dekho. Dono number lines ka mean same hai, red dashed line se marked. Upar Ramesh ki prices ek tight knot mein hain. Neeche Suresh ke dots door door corners mein bikhre hue hain.
Toh dispersion sirf ek fair tareeka hai ye poochhne ka: dots apne ghar se average mein kitni door rehte hain? Yahi ek sawaal poore chapter ko chalata hai.
Spread measure karne ke kai tareeke hain ek hierarchy mein, aur sabse crude tareeka hai range. Ye simply largest aur smallest observation ke beech ka gap hai.
Symbols mein, range equals x maximum minus x minimum. Bas itna hi, largest value mein se smallest ghatao, aur aapko data ki total width ka instant idea mil jaata hai.
Grouped ya continuous data ke liye ek chhota sa tweak hai. Highest class ki upper boundary lo aur lowest class ki lower boundary ghatao.
Range ek pehli nazar ke liye genuinely useful hai. Jab weather report bolti hai aaj temperature twenty two se forty one degrees tak raha, wo number din ke baare mein kuch real batata hai.

<chuckle>Lekin range thoda drama queen hai. Ye sirf do sabse extreme values ko sunta hai aur beech ki har cheez ko ignore kar deta hai. Ek freak observation, aur range poore set ke baare mein jhooth bol deta hai.
Alag alag scales ke data sets ko fairly compare karne ke liye hum coefficient of range use karte hain: x max minus x min, divided by x max plus x min. Same-unit quantities upar aur neeche.

Kyunki ye ek same-unit quantity ko doosri se divide karta hai, coefficient of range ek pure number hai, bina kisi unit ke. Isse aap rupees ki spread ko marks ki spread se ek level field pe compare kar sakte ho.
Range aapka lagbhag saara data waste kar deta hai. Ek smarter idea ye hai: har ek observation ke liye measure karo ki wo central value se kitni door hai, aur phir un saari distances ka average le lo.

Ab yahaan ek subtle move hai, aur ye ek word pe tika hai, distance. Ek value jo mean se paanch units neeche hai, utni hi spread out hai jitni ek jo paanch units upar hai. Direction matter nahi karni chahiye, sirf kitni door.
Isliye hum jaan boojh ke plus aur minus signs phenk dete hain. Hum har deviation ki absolute value lete hain. Minus five ka gap aur plus five ka gap, dono paanch ki distance count hote hain.
<whisper>Ye optional kyun nahi hai, suno. Mean se deviations hamesha, hamesha exactly zero mein add up hote hain, ye mean ki khud ki ek defining property hai.
Board pe likha dekh sakte ho: sum of x i minus x bar hamesha zero hai. Agar hum absolute value na lein, toh hamara spread measure duniya ke har data set ke liye zero report karega, bilkul useless.
Picture dekho. Ek chosen central point a se, har observation ek chhota sa arrow bhejta hai jiski length distance hai, x i minus a, absolute value mein.
Mean deviation in saari distance arrows ki average length se zyada kuch nahi hai. Yahi poora concept ek line mein.
Mean deviation range se ek real improvement hai, lekin ye do honest weaknesses ke saath aata hai jo aapko yaad rakhni chahiye.
Pehli mathematical hai. Absolute-value sign clumsy hai. Function mod x ka zero pe ek sharp corner hai, aur us point pe aap use cleanly differentiate nahi kar sakte.
Us corner ki wajah se, mean deviation aage ki algebra aur calculus mein fit hone se mana kar deta hai. Agar aap iske upar aur theory banana chaho toh ye ek dead end hai.

Aur yahi bilkul wajah hai ki agla subtopic mean deviation ko chhod ke variance aur standard deviation ki taraf jaata hai, jo deviations ki absolute value ke bajaye square lete hain, aur squaring har jagah smooth hai.
Doosri weakness: mean deviation utna hi meaningful hai jitna central value jispe aap use anchor karte ho. Same data set ka mean ke baare mein mean deviation, median ke baare mein alag hota hai.
Aur yahaan ek beautiful fact hai jo hum baad mein prove karenge, board pe likha hua: absolute deviations ka sum sabse chhota tab hota hai jab aap median ke baare mein measure karte ho.
<whisper>Toh deviation genuinely median ke baare mein sabse kam hota hai, mean ke baare mein nahi. Ye quiet fact bahut saare clever exam shortcuts ko power karta hai, toh abhi ise yaad kar lo.
Mean deviation compute kiya jaata hai, derive nahi, toh chalo ungrouped data ke liye exact step-by-step procedure pakadte hain, pehle mean ke baare mein.
Step one, mean nikalo. Ye aapka anchor hai, wo central value jisse har distance measure hogi. Anchor nahi, toh deviation nahi.
Mean hai x bar equals one over n times sum of all x i. Bas har observation ko jodo aur divide karo unki count se.

Step two, har absolute deviation banao, mod of x i minus x bar. Step three, un saari absolute deviations ko jodo taaki total scatter mile. Step four, n se divide karo taaki total scatter ek average ban jaaye.
Sab jod ke: mean deviation about the mean equals one over n, times sum of the absolute deviations. n se divide karna hi measure ko alag alag sizes ke data sets mein comparable banata hai.

Ab, median ke baare mein, procedure bilkul same hai ek change ke saath. Step one mein, mean ke bajaye, aap median nikaalte ho: data sort karo, odd n ke liye middle value lo, ya even n ke liye do middle values ka average lo.
Itni mehnat kyun? Kyunki median total absolute deviation ko minimise karta hai. Uske baare mein measure karne se aapko sabse chhoti, sabse honest mean deviation milti hai jo data de sakta hai.

segments.text: Now suppose the data doesn't come as a plain list, but as a frequency distribution, values with how often each one occurs. The procedure adapts in two small ways.
For a continuous distribution, your first job is to replace each class by a single representative value, its mid-point x i. For discrete data the x i are already given, so you skip this.
The mid-point is simply the lower limit plus the upper limit, all divided by two. It's the value that stands in for every observation inside that class.
Next you compute the weighted mean, then build the column f i times the absolute deviation, f i times mod x i minus x bar. Each distance gets multiplied by how many times its value occurs.
The formula on the board says it all: mean deviation about the mean equals one over N, times the sum of f i times the absolute deviations, where N is the total frequency, the sum of all the f i.
<whisper>Here is the single biggest trap in this whole subtopic. You divide by N, the total frequency, never by the number of classes or rows. Burn that into your memory.
And the reason for the f i weighting is pure common sense: an observation that occurs ten times must contribute its distance ten times, not once. The frequency is doing the counting for you.
There's one more case that trips students up: mean deviation about the median when the data is grouped. Here you cannot simply read the median off the table, you have to locate it.
Step one, build the cumulative frequency column, the running total of frequencies as you go down the classes.
Step two, identify the median class. It's the first class whose cumulative frequency reaches N over two, the halfway point of your total frequency.
Step three, compute the median by interpolation using this formula: M equals l, plus the quantity N over two minus C, divided by f, times h.
Let's name the pieces. l is the lower boundary of the median class. C is the cumulative frequency of the class just before it. f is the frequency of the median class itself. And h is its width.
Why interpolate at all? Because we assume the observations are spread evenly across the median class, so we step in proportionally to reach exactly the N over two-th value.
Once you have M, you proceed exactly like the frequency-distribution case, except you use mod x i minus M in place of mod x i minus x bar. The median just replaces the mean as the anchor.

Let's ground all that theory in a clean CBSE-level example. A student's marks in five class tests, out of forty, are thirty two, twenty eight, thirty six, twenty four, and thirty. We want the range and the mean deviation about the mean.
Read the problem carefully: two quantities to find, the range and the mean deviation about the mean, for these five marks.
The range comes first and it's instant. The largest mark is thirty six, the smallest is twenty four, so the range is thirty six minus twenty four, which is twelve marks.
Now the mean. Add all five marks, thirty two plus twenty eight plus thirty six plus twenty four plus thirty, that's one hundred fifty. Divide by five and the mean is exactly thirty.
Next, the absolute deviations from thirty. Thirty two is two away, twenty eight is two away, thirty six is six away, twenty four is six away, and thirty is zero away. So: two, two, six, six, zero.
Add those up to get sixteen, then divide by n, which is five. The mean deviation about the mean is sixteen over five, equals three point two marks.
Always finish with the presentation check. The answer carries the unit marks, and three point two is comfortably less than the range of twelve. Both boxes ticked, so the answer is consistent.
This JEE Main example hides the classic trap of the whole subtopic. A striker's goals per match are given as a frequency table, and we want the mean deviation of the number of goals about the mean.
The table on the board is your worksheet: goal counts zero to four, with frequencies four, six, eight, five, two. We'll work the whole thing in one sweep, column by column.

First, the total frequency N. Add the frequency column: four plus six plus eight plus five plus two, that's twenty five. This N is the number of matches, and it will be our divisor later, remember that.
Now the mean. The sum of f i times x i is zero, plus six, plus sixteen, plus fifteen, plus eight, which totals forty five. Divide by twenty five, and the mean is one point eight goals.

Next build the weighted absolute-deviation column, f i times mod x i minus one point eight. Those terms are seven point two, four point eight, one point six, six point zero, four point four. They add to twenty four point zero.
Finally, divide the twenty four by N. Mean deviation is twenty four over twenty five, equals zero point nine six goals.

<whisper>And here's the trap that costs marks. Under time pressure, students see five rows and divide twenty four by five, writing four point eight. Wrong. The divisor is N equals twenty five, the total from the frequency column, never the row count.

segments.text: Ab maano data ek plain list ki tarah nahi aata, balki ek frequency distribution ki tarah, values ke saath ki har ek kitni baar aati hai. Procedure do chhote tareekon se adapt hota hai.

Ek continuous distribution ke liye, aapka pehla kaam hai har class ko ek single representative value se replace karna, uska mid-point x i. Discrete data ke liye x i pehle se diye hote hain, toh ye skip karo.
Mid-point simply lower limit plus upper limit hai, poora divided by two. Ye wo value hai jo us class ke andar har observation ke liye khadi hoti hai.

Aage aap weighted mean compute karte ho, phir column banate ho f i times the absolute deviation, f i times mod x i minus x bar. Har distance ko multiply kiya jaata hai ki uski value kitni baar aati hai.
Board pe formula sab keh deta hai: mean deviation about the mean equals one over N, times sum of f i times the absolute deviations, jahan N total frequency hai, saare f i ka sum.
<whisper>Yahaan poore subtopic ka sabse bada trap hai. Aap N se divide karte ho, total frequency se, kabhi bhi classes ya rows ki number se nahi. Ise apni memory mein burn kar do.
Aur f i weighting ki wajah pure common sense hai: ek observation jo das baar aati hai use apni distance das baar contribute karni chahiye, ek baar nahi. Frequency aapke liye counting kar rahi hai.
Ek aur case hai jo students ko phasa deta hai: mean deviation about the median jab data grouped ho. Yahaan aap median ko simply table se padh nahi sakte, aapko use locate karna padta hai.

Step two, median class identify karo. Ye pehli class hai jiski cumulative frequency N over two tak pahunchti hai, aapki total frequency ka halfway point.

Chalo tukdon ko naam dete hain. l median class ki lower boundary hai. C us class se theek pehle wali class ki cumulative frequency hai. f khud median class ki frequency hai. Aur h uski width hai.

Jab M mil jaaye, aap bilkul frequency-distribution case ki tarah aage badhte ho, bas mod x i minus x bar ki jagah mod x i minus M use karte ho. Median bas anchor ke roop mein mean ki jagah le leta hai.

segments.text: This example connects dispersion with linear transformations, a favourite JEE Main theme. A set of monthly electricity bills has range forty and mean deviation about the mean twelve. The provider revises every bill by the rule y i equals three x i minus seven.
In plain terms, that's a three times tariff hike, then a seven rupee fixed rebate. We want the new range and the new mean deviation after this change.

Think of the rule as two moves: a shift and a scale. The shift is the minus seven, it moves every single bill down by the same amount, so all the gaps between bills stay exactly the same. Spread is completely blind to the shift.

The scale is the three. Multiplying every value by three stretches every gap by a factor of three. And both range and mean deviation are built purely out of gaps, so each one is multiplied by the absolute value of a.
So the new range is the absolute value of three, times the old range forty, which gives one hundred twenty.
And the new mean deviation is the absolute value of three, times the old twelve, which gives thirty six. Notice the minus seven never entered the calculation at all.

One elegant twist: had the rule been minus three x i minus seven, the answers would be identical, because only the absolute value of a matters. Flipping a data set about a point doesn't change how spread out it is.

Now a JEE Advanced gem that proves the median fact we promised earlier. For the observations seven, eleven, thirteen, sixteen, twenty, twenty four, define S of a as the sum of the absolute deviations from a. We must find where S is minimised, its minimum value, and every a that achieves it.
The data is already sorted, and n is six, an even number. Keep that evenness in mind, it makes the answer richer than a single point.
Here's the trick, the pairing argument. Pair the observations symmetrically from the outside in: seven with twenty four, eleven with twenty, thirteen with sixteen. Watch what each pair does.

Take the outer pair. For any a sitting between seven and twenty four, the two distances are mod a minus seven plus mod twenty four minus a, and that sum is always seventeen, a constant. Wherever a sits between them, the two distances trade off exactly.

The same holds for every pair, as long as a lies inside all three, which means a inside the innermost pair, the interval thirteen to sixteen. There, S of a is seventeen plus nine plus three, which is twenty nine.

The moment a leaves the interval thirteen to sixteen, it falls outside the innermost pair. That pair's contribution stops cancelling and starts to grow, so S of a strictly increases. Hence the minimum is twenty nine.

And the deep payoff: the minimiser is not a single point but the entire median interval, thirteen to sixteen. The conventional median, fourteen point five, sits right inside it. So if an Advanced problem asks how many values of a minimise S, the answer is infinitely many.
Let's do a full continuous-distribution computation, CBSE style. The daily wages of forty workers are grouped into five wage bands, and we want the mean deviation about the mean.

The table on the board is already set up. The first job on continuous data is to replace each wage class by its mid-point: one fifty, two fifty, three fifty, four fifty, and five fifty. Each mid-point is just the lower plus upper limit over two.

Now the weighted mean. The sum of f i times x i works out to thirteen thousand, and the total frequency N is forty workers. So the mean is thirteen thousand over forty, which is exactly three hundred twenty five.
With the mean in hand, build the f i times absolute-deviation column. The five entries are one thousand fifty, seven fifty, three fifty, one thousand, and four fifty.
Add that column: one thousand fifty plus seven fifty plus three fifty plus one thousand plus four fifty gives three thousand six hundred.
Finally divide by N. The mean deviation about the mean is three thousand six hundred over forty, which is ninety rupees.
And the same trap as before, made explicit: your divisor is N equals forty, the total number of workers, not the five wage classes. Grab N from the frequency total every single time.

The final worked example ties together interpolation and mean deviation about the median, a common JEE Main setup. The marks of forty students are grouped into five bands, and we want the mean deviation about the median.
Start by building the cumulative frequency column from the frequencies seven, eight, ten, nine, six. The running totals are seven, fifteen, twenty five, thirty four, forty.
Now locate the median class. N over two is twenty, and the first cumulative frequency to reach twenty is twenty five. That belongs to the class twenty to thirty, so that is our median class.

Interpolate. With l equals twenty, C equals fifteen the cumulative frequency before, f equals ten, and h equals ten, the median is twenty, plus twenty minus fifteen over ten, times ten, which is twenty plus five, equals twenty five.
With the median fixed at twenty five, build the column f i times mod x i minus twenty five, using the mid-points five, fifteen, twenty five, thirty five, forty five, exactly as the board table shows.
That column totals four hundred thirty. Divide by N, which is forty, and the mean deviation about the median is four hundred thirty over forty, equals ten point seven five marks.
<whisper>The watch-out here is fatal if missed: the median of grouped data is not the middle mid-point. You must interpolate it through the median class, or every single downstream number is wrong.

segments.text: Let's close Subtopic one with the four classic slips that quietly drain marks, and exactly how to dodge each.

Slip one: dropping the absolute-value sign. If you compute the sum of x i minus x bar without the modulus, you get exactly zero for every data set, because deviations about the mean always cancel. Students then wrongly conclude the mean deviation is zero. The modulus is the whole point.

Slip two, and this is the single biggest source of lost Board marks: the wrong divisor in frequency tables. The divisor is always N, the total frequency, the sum of the f i, never the number of rows or classes.

Slip three: using the mean when the question asks for the least mean deviation. If a question wants the smallest possible mean deviation, you anchor to the median, not the mean. Reading which central value is requested costs two seconds and saves the whole answer.

Slip four: believing a shift changes the spread. Adding or subtracting a constant changes neither the range nor any mean deviation. Only multiplying scales them, and it scales by the absolute value of a.

Lock in the transformation rule on the board: under x i maps to a x i plus b, both range and mean deviation map to the absolute value of a times the old value, and the plus b does nothing. Write it instantly, no recomputation needed.

And one final habit, your permanent sanity check before you commit any answer: the mean deviation must be smaller than the range. If it isn't, you have an arithmetic error upstream, go back and find it.
In the last subtopic we measured spread by averaging absolute deviations. It worked, but the modulus sign is mathematically grumpy, so let's see what statisticians did instead.
The problem is precise: mod x has a sharp corner at zero. You cannot differentiate it cleanly there, so it refuses to cooperate with the calculus and algebra that later chapters need.
Statisticians wanted a spread measure that kills the sign but stays smooth. Their trick is beautifully simple: instead of taking the absolute value of each deviation, they square it.

Squaring does three jobs at once. It throws away the sign, because a square is never negative. It is perfectly smooth, no corners. And crucially, it punishes large deviations far more than small ones.
The average of these squared deviations is the variance, written sigma squared: one over n, times the sum of x i minus x bar, all squared.

Picture each deviation as the side of a little square drawn on the number line. A point near the mean draws a tiny square; a far outlier draws an enormous one. Variance is the average area of all these squares.

See the arithmetic of that punishment: an observation two units from the mean contributes four, but one ten units away contributes one hundred, not ten. A single distant outlier can blow up the average area dramatically.
Variance has one real inconvenience, and standard deviation exists purely to fix it.
If your data is in marks, then the squared deviations are in marks squared, and so is the variance. Marks squared is an awkward unit nobody can actually interpret or picture.
The cure could not be simpler: take the positive square root of the variance. That drags the measure right back into the original units of the data.
That square root is the standard deviation, sigma, always the positive root. It is the single most-used measure of spread in all of statistics.

Here's why it matters. Two batsmen both average forty five runs. Batsman P scores forty four, forty six, forty five, forty three, forty seven, tight and dependable. Batsman Q scores five, ninety, twelve, eighty eight, thirty, wild swings around the same average.
For a must-win final you pick P, and the standard deviation is precisely the number that tells you P is the safer bet. Q's large sigma exposes the wild inconsistency the average alone hid.
Indian SIP investors run the very same logic. Two mutual funds may report identical average returns, but the one with the lower standard deviation is the calmer, steadier ride.
Standard deviation is great, but it hits a wall the moment you want to compare the consistency of two things measured on different scales.
The trouble is that sigma carries units. A spread of five kilograms and a spread of five centimetres are just not comparable numbers, so sigma alone cannot referee a heights-versus-weights contest.
The fix is to normalise. Divide the standard deviation by the mean, and multiply by one hundred to express it as a percentage. That strips away units and scale.
That gives the coefficient of variation: sigma over x bar, times one hundred. A single clean percentage for each series.

Because it is a pure number, the coefficient of variation compares apples to oranges, rupees against runs, heights against marks. And the rule is friendly: lower coefficient of variation means more consistent.

Think about why relative spread matters. A ten rupee swing is enormous on a fifty rupee item but completely invisible on a fifty thousand rupee item. Measuring spread relative to size captures exactly that difference.
So the verdict is always the same, and it's worth memorising: lower coefficient of variation means more consistent; higher coefficient of variation means more variable.

sections.title: Why variance is always measured about the mean & related topics

board_events.text: Variance sits on the mean — and only the mean
Unlike M.D. (which can sit on any centre), variance is always taken about the mean.
Why: just as the median minimises ∑|x_i − a|, the MEAN minimises the mean of squared deviations.
That's not a convention — it's a minimisation result (we prove it next).
Because of the squaring, variance is hypersensitive to outliers, so for skewed data it can overstate spread.
The only way to get zero variance is a perfectly flat data set.
The mean minimises mean-square deviation
Let g(a) = (1/n) ∑(x_i − a)². Minimise the average squared spread over the anchor a.
Set the derivative to zero to find the minimising anchor.
The mean is the UNIQUE anchor giving the smallest average squared spread.
Perfect parallel: median minimises absolute deviation; mean minimises squared deviation.
Coding big mid-points into tiny integers
Step 1: replace each class by its mid-point x_i.
Step 2: pick an assumed mean A (a central mid-point) and width h; code d_i = (x_i − A)/h.
Step 3: build the columns f_i d_i and f_i d_i², then their totals.
The h² (not h) undoes the coding — squared, because variance scales by the SQUARE of any factor.
Coding shrinks large mid-points to integers like −2… 2, slashing arithmetic error.
CBSE level: units sold on five days
Data: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24.  Find the variance and standard deviation.
Deviations: −6, −3, 0, 3, 6.  Squared: 36, 9, 0, 9, 36.  Sum = 90.
Units: variance in units², SD in units. And 4.24 ≤ range (12). Consistent.

segments.text: One structural fact separates variance from mean deviation, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising.
Mean deviation could be anchored to any central value, the mean, the median, or the mode. Variance is not so free. It is always measured about the mean, never anything else.
And that is not arbitrary. Recall from Subtopic one that the median minimises the sum of absolute deviations. The exact parallel holds here: the mean minimises the mean of the squared deviations.
So anchoring variance to the mean is not a convention someone chose for convenience. It is a genuine minimisation result, and we will prove it on the very next board.

One caution comes straight from the squaring. Variance is hypersensitive to outliers, because a single distant point contributes its distance squared. For heavily skewed data, variance can overstate the true spread.
And a clean boundary case, on the board: variance equals zero if and only if every single observation equals the mean.
In plain words, the only way to get zero variance is a perfectly flat data set where nothing varies at all. Any wobble at all makes sigma squared strictly positive.
We claimed the mean minimises the squared spread. Let's actually prove it, because the argument is short and the result anchors the whole subtopic.
Define a function g of a, equal to one over n times the sum of x i minus a, all squared. Here a is a free anchor, and we ask which value of a makes this average squared spread as small as possible.

Differentiate with respect to a. Bring the power down: g prime of a is one over n times the sum of two, times x i minus a, times minus one, which tidies to minus two over n times the sum of x i minus a.
To find the minimiser, set that derivative equal to zero. The constant factor minus two over n doesn't matter, so we just need the sum of x i minus a to vanish.
The sum of x i minus a equals zero means the sum of x i equals n times a, and dividing by n gives a equals x bar. So the minimising anchor is exactly the mean.
That is the whole point: the mean is the unique anchor that gives the smallest average squared spread. No other value of a can do better, which is why variance is always tied to the mean.
And notice the perfect parallel across the two subtopics. The median minimises absolute deviation; the mean minimises squared deviation. Two centres, two minimisation crowns.
For a grouped frequency distribution, computing variance by hand can get ugly fast. The step-deviation method exists to keep the arithmetic small and clean.
Step one is the usual move for continuous data: replace each class by its mid-point x i, one representative value per class.

segments.text: This is the single most common JEE Main statistics question, dressed up as a transformation. The variance of twenty observations is five. Each observation is transformed by the rule: multiply by three, then add four.
We're asked for the new variance and the new standard deviation after that rule is applied to every value.

Split the rule into a shift and a scale. The plus four shifts all the data equally, and a uniform shift cannot change spread at all. The times three is the scale, and that's what actually stretches the spread.
Here's the crucial bit. For variance, the scale factor does not enter as three, it enters squared. So a equals three contributes a factor of nine, not three.
Therefore the new variance is three squared times five, which is nine times five, equals forty five.

The new standard deviation is the absolute value of three times root five, which is three root five, approximately six point seven one. You could also just take the square root of forty five and get the same thing.

<whisper>And here's the signature trap. Students multiply the variance by three, getting fifteen, or fumble the square root. Lock it in: variance scales by a squared, standard deviation by the absolute value of a, and the additive constant does nothing.

This JEE Advanced classic tests whether you understand that combined spread is more than the parts. Section A has thirty students with mean sixty and standard deviation eight. Section B has twenty students with mean seventy and standard deviation six. Find the standard deviation of all fifty combined.
The whole trap lives in one temptation: you cannot just average the two standard deviations. The gap between the group means adds its own spread, and we have to account for it.
First, the combined mean. It's thirty times sixty plus twenty times seventy, all over fifty. That's thirty two hundred over fifty, equals sixty four.

Now measure how far each group's mean sits from that combined mean. d one is sixty minus sixty four, equals minus four. d two is seventy minus sixty four, equals six. These are the between-group deviations.

Apply the combined-variance formula. Each group contributes its own variance plus its d squared, weighted by its size: thirty times sixty four plus sixteen, plus twenty times thirty six plus thirty six, all over fifty. That's twenty four hundred plus fourteen forty, over fifty, equals seventy six point eight.
The combined standard deviation is the square root of seventy six point eight, approximately eight point seven six.

Now the insight worth the marks: the combined standard deviation, eight point seven six, is larger than either group's, eight and six. Pooling groups with different means injects extra spread through the d squared terms. A student who naively averages eight and six to get seven misses this entirely.
Let's finish the computation examples with the step-deviation method on grouped marks. Thirty students' marks fall into five bands of width twenty, and we want the variance and standard deviation.
The table on the board sets it all up. First replace each class by its mid-point, giving ten, thirty, fifty, seventy, ninety.

Now the coding. Take the assumed mean A as fifty, a central mid-point, and the width h as twenty. Then d i equals x i minus fifty, over twenty, which turns those mid-points into the tidy integers minus two, minus one, zero, one, two. Far less error-prone than the raw numbers.
Build and total the two coded columns. The sum of f i d i comes to minus one, and the sum of f i d i squared comes to forty one, as the table's total row shows.

Apply the step-deviation formula. Variance is h squared, that's twenty squared, or four hundred, times the bracket: forty one over thirty, minus the square of minus one over thirty. That works out to approximately five hundred forty six point two.
The standard deviation is the square root of that, approximately twenty three point four marks.

Two reminders. The h squared, four hundred, is what undoes the coding, and it's squared because variance scales by the square of any factor. And don't drop the tiny correction term, minus one over thirty squared, small as it is, because graders specifically look for it.
Let's close Subtopic two the same way, with the four classic slips that quietly cost marks, and exactly how to dodge each.

Slip one: confusing variance with standard deviation. They differ by a square root and by units, marks squared versus marks. Read the question carefully; if it asks for the standard deviation and you stop at variance, you lose the mark even with perfect working.

Slip two: mishandling the transformation rule. Under x maps to a x plus b, variance scales by a squared, standard deviation by the absolute value of a, and b is irrelevant. The classic slip is scaling variance by a instead of a squared.
Slip three: stopping the shortcut formula early. Students routinely forget the minus x bar squared at the end, or they subtract x bar instead of x bar squared. Either one wrecks the answer.

Keep the shortcut on the board in front of you: variance is one over n sum of x i squared, minus x bar squared. And here's a free diagnostic, if your variance comes out negative, you've swapped the two terms.

Slip four: averaging the standard deviations of two groups. The combined standard deviation is never the average of the parts. You must use the combined-variance formula, which adds the between-group d squared terms.

And two instant checks before you commit anything: variance must be at least zero, and the standard deviation must be no bigger than the range. For any consistency comparison, go straight to the coefficient of variation, and remember lower wins.

segments.text: The final subtopic answers the most practical question in the chapter: how do you compare the spread of two different groups?
A coach choosing between two batsmen, a buyer comparing two brands, an investor weighing two funds, they're all asking the same thing, which one is steadier?

Standard deviation alone can't always referee this. A spread of five rupees around a mean of fifty is a huge relative wobble, but a spread of five rupees around a mean of five thousand is almost nothing. Same sigma, completely different meaning.
So the fix is to measure spread relative to the size of what you're measuring. Divide the standard deviation by the mean, and multiply by one hundred to get a percentage.
That is the coefficient of variation: sigma over x bar, times one hundred. One clean percentage that captures relative spread.

The picture makes it visual. On the top bar, a sigma of five sits on a mean of forty, that's a big relative wobble, a high coefficient of variation. On the bottom bar, the very same sigma of five sits on a mean of two hundred, and it's a tiny relative wobble, a low coefficient of variation.

Because it's a pure ratio with no units, the coefficient of variation compares any two series at all, rupees against runs, heights against marks. And the rule stays friendly: lower coefficient of variation means more consistent.
Before you reach for the coefficient of variation on every problem, learn when it's actually needed, because sometimes it's overkill.
If the two groups have the same mean, the comparison is easy. Just compare their standard deviations directly, and the smaller sigma is the steadier group. No division needed.
But if the two groups have different means, or worse, different units, standard deviation alone cannot referee the contest. Here you must use the coefficient of variation.

Here's the key logical point, and examiners test it. When the means are equal, the coefficient of variation and the standard deviation give exactly the same ranking, because dividing both by the same mean can't change the order.
So the extra step of computing the coefficient of variation only earns its keep when the means genuinely differ. On equal means, it's just wasted arithmetic.
You can write the rule cleanly: if x bar one equals x bar two, compare sigma directly. Otherwise, go to the coefficient of variation.

<whisper>And here's the classic exam trap in this subtopic: comparing two series with different means by their standard deviations. A larger sigma does not mean more variable if the means differ. Normalise first.

The first master total comes straight from the mean. Since x bar is the sum of x i over n, the sum of x i must equal n times x bar. That converts a given mean into a hard number.

The second comes from the shortcut variance. Since sigma squared is the sum of x i squared over n, minus x bar squared, rearranging gives the sum of x i squared equals n times the quantity sigma squared plus x bar squared.
So every missing-observation problem and every correction problem is really just bookkeeping on these two numbers, the sum of the values and the sum of their squares.
And there's a clean reason they work. Two unknowns always need two independent constraints to pin them down, and the mean plus the variance supply exactly two.
The coefficient of variation is powerful, but it comes with fine print you must respect, or you'll apply it where it makes no sense.

First, it needs a non-zero mean. Since you're dividing by x bar, the coefficient of variation is simply undefined when the mean is zero, and it becomes wildly unstable and misleading when the mean is close to zero.
Second, it's meant for ratio data, data with a genuine, true zero. Heights, wages, and marks all qualify, because zero of each means a real absence of the quantity.

Third, and this one trips up strong students: more consistent, meaning a lower coefficient of variation, is not the same as better.
A consistent low scorer is still a low scorer. Consistency measures steadiness, not quality, so always read carefully what the question is actually rewarding.

board_events.text: A clean three-step comparison
Step 1: compute x̄ and σ for each series.
Step 2: if the means are equal, compare σ directly.
Step 3: the smaller C.V. is more consistent/stable; the larger C.V. is more variable.
Why divide by the mean: it converts an absolute wobble into a relative one — a fair comparison across scales.
Reverse form, if C.V. and σ are given: x̄ = (σ / C.V.) × 100.
Two unknowns, two equations
Step 1: turn the mean into ∑x_i = nx̄ — one equation in the unknowns.
Step 2: turn the variance into ∑(x_i − x̄)² = nσ² — a second equation.
Step 3: solve the two simultaneously.
From p+q (known) and p²+q² (known), the identity hands you the product pq — then roots of t²−(p+q)t+pq=0.
Two unknowns need two independent constraints; mean + variance are exactly those two.
Repair BOTH totals, not just the mean
Step 1: recover the wrong totals — ∑x = nx̄ and ∑x² = n(σ² + x̄²).
Step 3: recompute x̄ and σ from the repaired totals.
A wrong value pollutes BOTH ∑x (the mean) and ∑x² (the variance) — clean both.
If the value was omitted (not replaced): drop −w and −w² only, and reduce n by 1.
CBSE level: who is more consistent?
Arjun: mean 50 runs, SD 10.  Vikram: mean 40 runs, SD 6.  Different means → use C.V.
Lower C.V. → Vikram is the more consistent scorer.
But Arjun's higher average (50 vs 40) makes him the better bet to chase a steep total.
“Consistent” and “best” are different questions — this split verdict is exactly what examiners test.

segments.text: Let's turn all that intuition into a clean, repeatable procedure for comparing two distributions.
Step one, compute both summary numbers for each series, the mean x bar and the standard deviation sigma. You need both before you can decide anything.
Step two, check the means. If the two means are equal, you can compare the standard deviations directly and you're done, no coefficient of variation needed.
Otherwise, when the means differ, compute the coefficient of variation for each series: sigma over x bar, times one hundred. That's the fair yardstick when the scales differ.
Step three, read the verdict. The series with the smaller coefficient of variation is more consistent and stable; the larger one is more variable.
Always know why you're dividing by the mean: it converts an absolute wobble into a relative one, which is what makes the comparison fair across different scales in the first place.

And keep one algebraic cousin handy for reverse problems. If a question gives you the coefficient of variation and the standard deviation, you can recover the mean: x bar equals sigma over the coefficient of variation, times one hundred.
Now the procedure for the most popular JEE Main reverse problem, finding missing observations when you're told the mean and the variance.

Step one, translate the given mean into the first master total. The sum of x i equals n times x bar. With three known values and two unknowns, this gives you one equation, the unknowns sum to a fixed number.

Step two, translate the given variance. The sum of squared deviations, x i minus x bar all squared, equals n times sigma squared. Subtract off the known observations' contributions, and you get a second equation in the two unknowns.
Step three, solve the two equations simultaneously. You now know the sum of the two unknowns and the sum of their squared deviations, which is enough to pin them both down.
The neat shortcut uses the algebraic identity: p plus q, all squared, equals p squared plus q squared, plus two p q. You already know p plus q and p squared plus q squared.
So the identity hands you the product p q directly. With the sum and the product in hand, p and q are just the roots of a quadratic, t squared minus the sum times t, plus the product, equals zero.
The reason this always closes is the same as before: two unknowns need two independent constraints, and the mean and the variance are exactly those two constraints.
The last procedure repairs a data set after a value was recorded wrongly, and the whole art is in remembering to clean two totals, not one.

Step one, recover the wrong totals from the reported statistics. The wrong sum of x is n times the wrong mean, and the wrong sum of x squared is n times the quantity wrong variance plus wrong mean squared.

Step two for the sum: subtract the wrong value's contribution and add the correct one's. The corrected sum of x equals the wrong sum, minus w, plus c, where w is the wrong value and c is the correct value.
Step two for the sum of squares: do the identical repair but with squares. The corrected sum of x squared equals the wrong sum of squares, minus w squared, plus c squared.
Step three, recompute the mean and standard deviation from the two repaired totals, and you have your corrected answers.

Here is the reasoning that stops students losing half the marks: a single wrong value polluted both the sum of x, which drives the mean, and the sum of x squared, which drives the variance. You must clean both, fixing only the mean is the most common half-mark loss.
One variation to watch. If the value was omitted entirely rather than replaced, you drop only the minus w and minus w squared, and you reduce n by one, since there's one fewer observation.

A perfect CBSE example to show that the coefficient of variation answers one question, but not every question. Batsman Arjun averages fifty runs with a standard deviation of ten. Batsman Vikram averages forty runs with a standard deviation of six. Who is more consistent, and who would you pick to chase a steep total?
The means differ, fifty versus forty, so standard deviation alone can't referee. We go straight to the coefficient of variation for each.
Arjun's coefficient of variation is ten over fifty, times one hundred, which is twenty percent.
Vikram's is six over forty, times one hundred, which is fifteen percent. Lower, so far so good.
Since fifteen percent is lower than twenty percent, Vikram is the more consistent scorer. If the question stopped at consistency, Vikram wins outright.
But consistency isn't everything. Arjun's higher average, fifty versus forty, makes him the better bet to chase a steep total, where raw run-scoring power matters more than steadiness.
That split verdict is exactly what examiners love to test. Consistent and best are two different questions, so read carefully which one is being asked before you commit your answer.

First equation, from the mean. The five values must sum to five times six, which is thirty. So two plus four plus nine plus a plus b equals thirty, giving a plus b equals fifteen.

Second equation, from the variance. The sum of squared deviations about the mean six equals five times six point eight, which is thirty four. The three known values contribute sixteen plus four plus nine, so a minus six squared plus b minus six squared equals five.

Now substitute to make it clean. Let p be a minus six and q be b minus six. Then p plus q is fifteen minus twelve, which is three, and p squared plus q squared is five. Using the identity, three squared equals five plus two p q, so p q equals two.

With sum three and product two, p and q are the roots of t squared minus three t plus two equals zero, which factors to give t equals one and two. Undoing the substitution, a and b are seven and eight.

Always verify. The five observations two, four, nine, seven, eight have mean thirty over five, which is six, and variance sixteen plus four plus nine plus one plus four, over five, which is thirty four over five, exactly six point eight. Both boxes ticked.

This example shows exactly why you must repair both totals in a correction problem. For twenty observations, the mean and standard deviation were found to be thirty and five. On rechecking, a value recorded as fifty is actually thirty. Find the corrected mean and standard deviation.
The plan: recover the two wrong totals, repair each one, then recompute. Watch how the sum of squares does its own separate repair.

First the wrong totals. The wrong sum of x is twenty times thirty, which is six hundred. The wrong sum of x squared is twenty times the quantity five squared plus thirty squared, that's twenty times nine hundred twenty five, equals eighteen thousand five hundred.

Repair the sum of x: subtract the wrong fifty and add the correct thirty. Six hundred minus fifty plus thirty is five hundred eighty, so the corrected mean is five hundred eighty over twenty, which is twenty nine.

It's a two-stage problem: first combine to get the pooled variance, then normalise to get the coefficient of variation. Take them in order.
First the combined mean. It's forty times sixty plus sixty times fifty, all over one hundred. That's five thousand four hundred over one hundred, equals fifty four.
Now the group-mean deviations from that combined mean. d one is sixty minus fifty four, equals six. d two is fifty minus fifty four, equals minus four. These carry the between-group spread.

Apply the combined-variance formula. Each group contributes its variance plus its d squared, weighted by size: forty times sixty four plus thirty six, plus sixty times thirty six plus sixteen, all over one hundred. That's four thousand plus three thousand one hundred twenty, over one hundred, equals seventy one point two.

So the combined standard deviation is the square root of seventy one point two, about eight point four four. And the combined coefficient of variation is eight point four four over fifty four, times one hundred, roughly fifteen point six percent.

Note the same lesson as before, now with different numbers: the combined standard deviation, eight point four four, exceeds both group standard deviations, eight and six. Pooling groups with different means injects extra spread through the d squared terms, which a careless average-the-SDs approach would completely miss.

segments.text: Let's pause and lay out every formula from this subtopic in one place. This is your complete toolkit, I'm restating, not re-teaching, so treat this as a quick reference board.
At the top, the range is x max minus x min. And the coefficient of range is that same difference, x max minus x min, over their sum, x max plus x min, a pure number.
For ungrouped data, mean deviation about any central value a is one over n, times the sum of the absolute deviations mod x i minus a.
For a frequency distribution, it's one over N, times the sum of f i times mod x i minus a, where N is the total frequency, the sum of the f i. Same idea, weighted by frequency.
The coefficient of mean deviation is just the mean deviation divided by the central value a. Like the coefficient of range, it's dimensionless, handy for comparing across scales.
And when you need the median of grouped data, use the interpolation formula: M equals l, plus N over two minus C, over f, times h.

Two things to memorise, in red. The sum of absolute deviations is least at the median. And your permanent sanity check: mean deviation can never exceed the range. If it does, you've made an arithmetic slip.
This is a standard CBSE board derivation, and it produces the formula you'll actually use in almost every numerical, so follow each step.

Start from the definition and expand the square inside the sum. Sigma squared is one over n times the sum of x i minus x bar squared, which expands to x i squared, minus two x bar x i, plus x bar squared.
The reason we expand is to separate the data-dependent part, the sum of x i squared, from the constant mean, so we never have to compute individual deviations.

Now split the sum into three pieces. This is legal because summation distributes over addition. You get one over n sum of x i squared, minus two x bar over n times sum of x i, plus one over n sum of x bar squared.

Use two facts. First, one over n times the sum of x i is exactly x bar, so the middle term becomes minus two x bar times x bar, which is minus two x bar squared. Second, x bar squared is a constant, so its sum is n x bar squared, and the last term collapses to just x bar squared.
Combine minus two x bar squared plus x bar squared, and you land on the workhorse: sigma squared equals one over n sum of x i squared, minus x bar squared.
This form is the one to reach for, because it avoids computing a single individual deviation. It's especially valuable when the mean turns out not to be a whole number.

At the core: variance is one over n sum of x i minus x bar squared, and equivalently the shortcut, one over n sum of x i squared minus x bar squared. Standard deviation is the positive square root of variance.
For a frequency distribution, variance is one over N sum of f i x i squared, minus the square of sum of f i x i over N, where N is the total frequency.
For grouped data by coding, variance is h squared times the bracket, sum of f i d i squared over N minus the square of sum of f i d i over N, with d i equal to x i minus A, over h.

Two must-knows for MCQs. The coefficient of variation is sigma over x bar times one hundred. And under the transformation x maps to a x plus b, variance scales by a squared, standard deviation by the absolute value of a, and b does nothing.

For two combined groups: variance equals n one times sigma one squared plus d one squared, plus n two times sigma two squared plus d two squared, all over n one plus n two, where each d is the group mean minus the combined mean.

Finally, in red: a standard result worth memorising, the variance of the first n natural numbers is n squared minus one, over twelve. And your permanent sanity checks, variance is never negative, and sigma never exceeds the range.

Now watch why the shortcut formula earns its keep. We need the variance of a frequency distribution where x i takes values four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, with frequencies two, five, eight, three, two.
The table on the board is the whole strategy. We build two columns in one sweep: f i times x i, and f i times x i squared. No deviations anywhere.

First the mean. The total frequency N is twenty. The sum of f i x i is two hundred thirty two, so the mean is two hundred thirty two over twenty, equals eleven point six. Notice that's not a whole number, which is exactly when the shortcut shines.

Next, the sum of f i x i squared. Adding the last column, thirty two plus three hundred twenty plus one thousand one hundred fifty two plus seven hundred sixty eight plus eight hundred, gives three thousand seventy two.

Now apply the shortcut. Variance is the sum of f i x i squared over N, minus x bar squared: three thousand seventy two over twenty, minus eleven point six squared. That's one hundred fifty three point six, minus one hundred thirty four point five six, equals nineteen point zero four.
The standard deviation is the square root of nineteen point zero four, approximately four point three six.
The payoff is clear: with the mean at eleven point six, computing every deviation would have meant ugly decimals like x i minus eleven point six. The shortcut let us avoid all of them.
Here's the compact toolkit for this subtopic, gathered in one place for quick recall. I'm restating the tools, not re-teaching them.

At the top, the coefficient of variation is sigma over x bar times one hundred, valid whenever the mean isn't zero. And its reverse form recovers the mean: x bar equals sigma over the coefficient of variation, times one hundred.
The two master totals, the engine of every reverse problem: the sum of x i equals n times x bar, and the sum of x i squared equals n times the quantity sigma squared plus x bar squared.
For a correction, repair both totals: the corrected sum of x is the wrong sum minus w plus c, and the corrected sum of x squared is the wrong sum of squares minus w squared plus c squared.

For two missing observations, use the identity p plus q all squared equals p squared plus q squared plus two p q to get the product, then solve the quadratic t squared minus the sum times t, plus the product, equals zero.

And the combined-group formulas carried over from before: the combined mean is the frequency-weighted average of the two means, and the combined variance adds each group's own variance and its squared mean-gap, weighted by size.

Finally, three quick guardrails in red: if the means are equal, skip the coefficient of variation and just compare sigma; a corrected variance must stay at least zero; and the coefficient of variation is always dimensionless.

Coefficient of mean deviation bas mean deviation divided by central value a hai. Coefficient of range ki tarah, ye dimensionless hai, alag scales pe compare karne ke liye handy.
Aur jab aapko grouped data ka median chahiye, interpolation formula use karo: M equals l, plus N over two minus C, over f, times h.

Definition se shuru karo aur sum ke andar square expand karo. Sigma squared one over n times sum of x i minus x bar squared hai, jo expand hoke banta hai x i squared, minus two x bar x i, plus x bar squared.
Expand karne ki wajah ye hai ki hum data-dependent part, sum of x i squared, ko constant mean se alag kar sakein, taaki humein kabhi individual deviations compute na karni padein.

Ab sum ko teen tukdon mein baanto. Ye legal hai kyunki summation addition pe distribute hota hai. Milta hai one over n sum of x i squared, minus two x bar over n times sum of x i, plus one over n sum of x bar squared.

Do facts use karo. Pehla, one over n times sum of x i exactly x bar hai, toh middle term ban jaata hai minus two x bar times x bar, jo hai minus two x bar squared. Doosra, x bar squared ek constant hai, toh iska sum n x bar squared hai, aur aakhri term collapse hoke sirf x bar squared reh jaata hai.
Minus two x bar squared plus x bar squared ko jodo, aur aap workhorse pe pahunchte ho: sigma squared equals one over n sum of x i squared, minus x bar squared.
Yahi form pakadna chahiye, kyunki ye ek bhi individual deviation compute karne se bacha leta hai. Ye khaas taur pe tab valuable hai jab mean whole number na nikle.

Do combined groups ke liye: variance equals n one times sigma one squared plus d one squared, plus n two times sigma two squared plus d two squared, poora over n one plus n two, jahaan har d group mean minus combined mean hai.

Aakhir mein, red mein: ek standard result yaad rakhne layak, first n natural numbers ka variance n squared minus one, over twelve hai. Aur aapke permanent sanity checks, variance kabhi negative nahi hota, aur sigma kabhi range se zyada nahi hota.

Ab dekho shortcut formula apni jagah kyun banata hai. Humein ek frequency distribution ka variance chahiye jahaan x i values leta hai four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty, frequencies two, five, eight, three, two ke saath.
Board pe table poori strategy hai. Hum do columns ek sweep mein banate hain: f i times x i, aur f i times x i squared. Kahin koi deviations nahi.

Pehle mean. Total frequency N twenty hai. Sum of f i x i two hundred thirty two hai, toh mean two hundred thirty two over twenty hai, equals eleven point six. Dhyan do ye whole number nahi hai, aur theek tab shortcut chamakta hai.

Aage, sum of f i x i squared. Aakhri column jodte hue, thirty two plus three hundred twenty plus one thousand one hundred fifty two plus seven hundred sixty eight plus eight hundred, deta hai three thousand seventy two.

Ab shortcut apply karo. Variance sum of f i x i squared over N hai, minus x bar squared: three thousand seventy two over twenty, minus eleven point six squared. Ye hai one hundred fifty three point six, minus one hundred thirty four point five six, equals nineteen point zero four.
Standard deviation nineteen point zero four ka square root hai, lagbhag four point three six.
Payoff clear hai: mean eleven point six pe hone se, har deviation compute karne ka matlab hota ugly decimals jaise x i minus eleven point six. Shortcut ne humein un sab se bacha liya.

Do master totals, har reverse problem ka engine: sum of x i equals n times x bar, aur sum of x i squared equals n times the quantity sigma squared plus x bar squared.
Ek correction ke liye, dono totals repair karo: corrected sum of x wrong sum minus w plus c hai, aur corrected sum of x squared wrong sum of squares minus w squared plus c squared hai.

Do missing observations ke liye, identity p plus q poora squared equals p squared plus q squared plus two p q use karke product nikaalo, phir quadratic solve karo t squared minus the sum times t, plus the product, equals zero.

Aur pehle se aaye combined-group formulas: combined mean do means ka frequency-weighted average hai, aur combined variance har group ka apna variance aur uska squared mean-gap jodta hai, size se weighted.
